Western Yellowjacket (Vespula pensylvanica) is native across the western half of North America. They are both carnivore and herbivore. V. pensylvanica can usually be differentiated from other species of social wasps in the genus Vespula by the continuous yellow ring (often referred to as an eye-loop) present around each eye. The eye-loop is not always present. Though few females lack this distinguishing characteristic, males often do not have the eye-loop. In such cases, V. pensylvanica can be identified by a spotted mark on the frons below the antenna, a slender aedeagus, and a denser apical region of tergum 7. The fore wing length ranges from 8.5-10.5 mm for workers, 12.5-14.5 mm for females, and 12.5-14.0 mm for males.
Western yellowjackets build large nests made of wood fibers, enclosed in a hexagonal paper envelope with a small 10– to 30-cm entrance tunnel at the bottom. Nests are usually found 10–15 cm below ground or in other dark cavities, such as rodent burrows.https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/61355-Vespula-pensylvanica

description:
In my 30+ years of living, I've never been stung by a flying insect. On this day, I accidentally rolled my lawnmower over a ground nest and got stung 12+ times. I ran into the house, and immediately disrobed. At least 6 wasps were stuck to my shirt, and tossing the shirt on the floor only made them angrier. As soon as the wasps freed themselves from the crumpled garment, they continued to terrorize me (chase me around the house). 

After a terrifying battle, I managed to neutralize all the intruders. My next step (after sleeping off 4 Benadryl) was to head to Lowes.

I set two traps within 15' of where I left my lawnmower, and haven't cut my yard since 😩😩

Last week (about a month later) I went out to check the traps. I saw a hoard yellowjackets swarming around the trap, so I left them alone and went back inside. I assumed that I was far enough away that I didn't disturb them, but I was wrong. Later that evening, as I was getting ready for bed, a wasp flew into my bedroom making a "beeline" straight for me, and accomplished it's mission (stung me again) then flew to the closest window, trying to make an exit (they were not successful.)

These little guys truly stand up to their reputation; pesky, relentless hell spawn that never forget.

It took me 36 years to be stung by something and in the last 6 weeks I've been stung 17x.

Thank Goodness I'm not allergic (I've been told that I was my whole life.)

description:
This one is for the wasp
Photo 1:
Assassin Bug vs Yellowjacket
I was walking along a creek bank when I noticed a lot of frantic activity going on in the vegetation. I was able to quickly grab a few hurried shots before it was all over. An assassin bug had just grabbed an unsuspecting yellowjacket & the wasp was fighting for its life. Both are aggressive predators with venom that they inject. They are face to face in this shot.
Photo 2:
Life & Death Struggle
The wasp was struggling to get away, did not see a sting attempt. The assassin bug was trying to hang onto the wasp long enough to insert its tube-like proboscis and inject venom.
Photo 3:
Desperation
Lucky shot a split second before the assassin bug dropped the wasp. The weight of the struggling wasp dangling in the air was just too heavy for the bug. The wasp hit the ground then flew away. The assassin bug looked down a moment then scrambled back into hiding in the vegetation. No meal this time.

description:
Worker appears to be pulling our potential pupa from the colony for likely disposal.  I had recorded two minutes of video of those entering and exiting, and two others appeared to be taking debris, possibly body parts, out of the colony opening.

A few weeks back, I would see workers emerging with dirt, I assume as part of both maintenance and expansion.  I seemed to notice grayer material being removed more often as time went on, perhaps part of the cell  structures.  It's possible they've been moving more debris I've just not noticed, often I don't have time to review daily videos I take in real-time, and assumed I might get to it in the offseason.

I would say the traffic in/out of the colony has dropped by a factor of 5-10 by now, with only one coming/goign about every 4 seconds, and suspect the end is quite near.

I've seen three distinct nests within 50-70' or so (one just 12' away), but I can only stand directly over this colony's interest.  I did this with another ground colony several years ago, and they disappeared last week of November, but elevation was a bit higher.

Brief slomo taken instead with my iPhone held a few inches over nest (probably would not have tried a month ago when traffic volume was so much higher... as it was then they were buzzing past my head in both directions.  I've speculated they sometimes start hanging around a bit more between my body and the colony entrance, perhaps picking up on increased CO2 levels, which in some cases might be a predator, but I learned to monitor their activity closely, and fortunately it does not cause me stress, or I would leave for fear or pheromones I might also be giving off!

description:
Continuous yellow eye-loop present around each eye = Western Yellowjacket.

Western Yellowjacket (Vespula pensylvanica) is native across the western half of North America. They are both carnivore and herbivore. V. pensylvanica can usually be differentiated from other species of social wasps in the genus Vespula by the continuous yellow ring (often referred to as an eye-loop) present around each eye. The eye-loop is not always present. Though few females lack this distinguishing characteristic, males often do not have the eye-loop. In such cases, V. pensylvanica can be identified by a spotted mark on the frons below the antenna, a slender aedeagus, and a denser apical region of tergum 7. The fore wing length ranges from 8.5-10.5 mm for workers, 12.5-14.5 mm for females, and 12.5-14.0 mm for males.
Western yellowjackets build large nests made of wood fibers, enclosed in a hexagonal paper envelope with a small 10– to 30-cm entrance tunnel at the bottom. Nests are usually found 10–15 cm below ground or in other dark cavities, such as rodent burrows.https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/61355-Vespula-pensylvanica

An Outside School family reported that they had walked down a trail over the weekend that we use most days, and two of the four of them got stung. A parent offered to show me where it happened, and got stung on the belly as we walked down the trail. 

The next day I had this idea that I wanted to get to the bottom of who stung them. So, the kids waited by the creek, having gone down the wider trail, while I went up to the area shown to me yesterday with an insect net. Nothing appeared, so I tapped some trees and branches. Still nothing. I tapped harder, and I got swarmed! I swished my insect net back and forth, hoping to catch some of the insects. And I got stung on both ears! I managed to flip the net over, trapping several insects, and ran down the hill, as I was being chased. The kids ran away fast! Later, I got stung in the back of my neck because one had become stuck in my hair. 

The net and the terrarium have one tiny hole apiece, so eventually they all got out. They look a lot like yellow jackets, but closer to honeybee size. So, I don't know exactly what it was. It looks like there are a few different yellow jacket species in California, but I haven't looked too far into it.

When I saw one of the rangers, I told him about our discovery. And when we all finished at the bathroom for snack, a kid took photos of my ear and neck bites so I could see. They saw a stinger in one of the stings. Since that needed to come out, one kid took it out with the pliers, preventing a walk back to my car for tweezers, and another videotaped the process. It was faster and simpler than we all thought!

description:
A bit discouraged and disheartened today, but I was also super busy -- I got to spend some time outside to clear my mind a bit!  
Of course, I got to spend a good amount of time at Ladd Nature Preserve before the master plan meeting this evening.  Had a great time!

This is a female worker of the social wasp species *Vespula pensylvanica*, seen nectaring at flowers of Eriogonum nudum. Note that the thoracic and abdominal color patterns are similar for female workers of *V. pensylvanica* and *V. germanica* (compare 1st photo here with the 2nd column of images here and here). However a principal diagnostic character separating the two species is that the eyes of *V. pensylvanica* are usually entirely surrounded by a yellow margin or "eye loop" (compare 2nd & 3rd photos above with reference images here and here); whereas in *V. germanica* the inner edges of the eyes near the ocelli are black (cf. here and here). For further info, see the excellent Wikipedia *Vespula pensylvanica* page, and also the BugGuide *V. pensylvanica* and *V. germanica* pages.

description:
It was a few minutes before sunset when I noticed a wasp hanging on the north-facing stucco wall about a meter above the ground. I’m not an entomologist, but I am familiar with paper wasps. This one looked different. I researched the identity of the vespid and confirmed it’s a queen yellow jacket. Typically, the colony dies off as it gets colder in the fall. The queen hibernates (overwinters). In the spring, she rebuilds the underground nest and starts a new colony. 

Other ways to identify a queen are by size: this one is roughly 18 mm (⁷⁄₁₀”), about 50% bigger than workers. She has a distinct yellow ring (eye-loop) around the dark eyes. There are black dots along each side of yellow bands on its abdomen (alternating with narrowing black bands as it reaches the tip).

It was a mild winter day. The temperature plummeted from a high of 60°F to 50°F when I started taking photos to 45°F upon finishing. I took the first shots while the yellow jacket was on the wall. I went inside and came back out to carefully relocate the queen onto a plate with a swab of sugar under a cover where it was a bit warmer. She began to move slowly. I let her on my hand and arm, then gently returned her to the plate. The queen fluttered her wings. A minute later, she flew off.
